source: MAFF training slide deck: "ការបញ្ជាក់គុណភាពគ្រាប់ពូជ" (Seed Quality Verification), presented by Mr. Pang Sokha, Seed Management and Development Office, 28 Nov 2014. No elibrary URL visible in the source file — this is a training presentation, not a library document.
text:
Cambodia's seed certification system sorts rice seed (ក្រាប់ពូជ, kroab pouch) into a chain of quality grades, each one step further from the original breeder's plant material. From highest to lowest control: Breeder Seed (ពូជសុទ្ធជម្រើសវិទូ), Foundation Seed (ពូជសុទ្ធគ្រឹះ, FS), Registered Seed (ពូជសុទ្ធទទួលស្គាល់, RS), Certified Seed (ពូជសុទ្ធអនុញ្ញាត, CS), and Good Seed (ពូជសុទ្ធល្អ, GS) — GS being the everyday quality farmers typically buy or multiply themselves. Seed quality depends on several things happening correctly at every stage: the physical shape and structure of the grain, the crop's genetic characteristics, growing conditions (temperature, soil fertility, environment), and how carefully the seed is handled during harvest, post-harvest work, and storage.

Each grade has its own minimum/maximum limits, checked during seed testing:

- Purity (minimum): FS 98%, RS 98%, CS 98%, GS 95%
- Other crop seed mixed in (maximum): FS 2%, RS 2%, CS 2%, GS 5%
- Weed seed content (maximum): FS 0.05%, RS 0.05%, CS 0.10%, GS 0.50%
- Seeds of other unwanted plant species (maximum): FS 0.05%, RS 0.10%, CS 0.22%, GS 3%
- Off-type/mixed-variety seed (maximum): FS 0.05%, RS 0.10%, CS 0.20%, GS 2%
- Germination rate (minimum): 85% for all four grades
- Moisture content (maximum): FS 12%, RS 12%, CS 13%, GS 14%

In short: as you move from Foundation Seed down to Good Seed, the allowed impurity, off-type, and moisture limits loosen slightly, while the minimum germination requirement (85%) stays the same across all grades. A farmer buying certified seed for planting should expect at least these standards; anything worse suggests poor-quality or mislabeled seed.

A handful of practices are what actually keep seed at these quality levels in the field: always multiplying seed according to its labeled grade rather than mixing grades together; being strict about preventing variety mix-up at every stage — seedbed, active growth, flowering, and grain-filling; careful harvesting and threshing; proper sun-drying and cleaning before storage; correct packaging; and dry, pest-free warehouse storage afterward. A weak link at any one of these stages can drop otherwise good seed down a grade or make it unfit for planting.

(Note on precision: the percentage limits above are copied from the training slide's summary table and should be treated as the official reference values for that grade; if you are using this for formal seed certification decisions, cross-check against the current official MAFF seed standard document.)
